stops.note: 'appearance, imagination', from phainein 'to show'; Aristotle's On the Soul analyses phantasia as the mind's power to form images
Quintilian recommends the orator summon vivid phantasiae, mental pictures, to move an audience
via Old French fantasie English first got 'fantasy', and 'fancy' is its contraction; Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice (c. 1597) asks 'Tell me where is fancy bred'

current_meaning: elaborate or decorative; a liking or whim; to want or imagine
